paper_title: Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM: Benchmarking Multimodal Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Forgery Pipelines

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Audio-visual deepfakes can spread misinformation and enable impersonation, undermining trust in digital media. However, existing datasets provide limited coverage of forgery operations and their combinations, constraining detector development and systematic evaluation. We introduce Mega-MMDF, containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips across 22 pipelines spanning modality-specific manipulations, stacked forgeries, and joint audio-video generation. To assess its training value and enable fair comparisons, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, which standardizes training and evaluation across 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Training-based detectors achieve their highest mean AUC when trained on Mega-MMDF, with gains of up to 0.0784 over the best alternative training dataset for each detector. Experiments on data scale and pipeline coverage further support the value of large, diverse training data. Cross-pipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric generalization. Training on composite forgeries does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. Our analysis of altered inputs shows that modality masking can increase false alarms and missed detections, and temporal misalignment can raise mean predicted forgery probabilities. Together, these resources provide a foundation for understanding and improving multimodal deepfake detection, with publicly available code and dataset access subject to application and usage terms.

While unimodal detectors examine forgery artifacts in audio [10][13] or visual content [14][21] separately, multimodal approaches [22][29] can additionally exploit relationships between the two modalities. Existing audio-visual deepfake datasets provide resources for detector training and evaluation [30][34]. In particular, the AVDeepfake1M series [35], [36] has expanded these resources to the million scale. However, existing datasets cover limited range of forgery methods and pipelines, and many are also limited in scale. Specifically, forgery method denotes specific generation or manipulation algorithm, whereas forgery pipeline specifies the selection and ordering of forgery operations, each implemented by corresponding method. As audio-visual content can undergo individual operations or compositions of multiple operations, limited forgery pipeline coverage restricts the conditions represented in training and evaluation. These limitations motivate large-scale dataset with broader coverage of forgery methods and pipelines. To address this need, we introduce Mega-MMDF, million-scale audio-visual deepfake dataset containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips. Its construction uses 10 audio forgery methods, 12 visual forgery methods, 6 audio-driven face reenactment methods, and 2 joint audio-video generation methods. We organize these components into pipelines with the aim of maintaining correspondence between speech content and visible articulation, applying audio-driven face reenactment where needed. The resulting 22 forgery pipelines cover manipulations of individual modalities, compositions of multiple operations, and joint audio-video generation. Beyond providing training data, pipeline identities and modalityspecific authenticity annotations support systematic evaluation of detection coverage and cross-pipeline generalization. To evaluate Mega-MMDFs training value and characterize detector behavior, we need reproducible comparisons under consistent experimental settings. However, limited access to training implementations and differences in evaluation protocols in existing works make transparent and reproducible comparisons difficult. We therefore develop DeepfakeBench-MM, unified and extensible benchmark supporting eight datasets and ten multimodal deepfake detectors. Its modular framework integrates detector implementations with standardized data processing, explicit training configurations, and shared 1In this work, multimodal content refers specifically to audio-visual content. Preprint 2 evaluation protocols while accommodating detector-specific input requirements. Our evaluations based on DeepfakeBenchMM show that training on Mega-MMDF achieves the highest average clip-level AUC score over eight test datasets for all seven training-based detectors. Data-scale experiments show that larger subsets of Mega-MMDF generally improve detection performance. Pipeline-wise evaluations further show that training on individual pipelines does not provide consistently strong detection across forgery conditions, highlighting the value of the diverse pipeline coverage provided by MegaMMDF. Within DeepfakeBench-MM, Mega-MMDF also supports systematic analysis of how detectors generalize across forgery pipelines and respond to changes in input conditions. Crosspipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric transfer, showing that training on composite pipeline does not necessarily enable detection of its constituent operations in isolation. Zero-filling missing modality can increase false alarms on authentic clips and missed detections of forgeries in the retained modality. When both modalities remain available, disrupting their temporal correspondence in authentic clips produces detector-dependent prediction changes. These findings motivate broader forgery coverage, reliable handling of missing modalities, and further investigation of how audiovisual correspondence should complement modality-specific authenticity evidence. RELATED WORK A. Multimodal Deepfake Detectors Unimodal deepfake detectors identify synthesis artifacts in either audio [10][13] or visual content [14][21], [37], [38]. In contrast, multimodal detectors use both modalities to capture intra-modal artifacts and cross-modal relations. Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into four categories. a) Aggregation of modality-specific representations and predictions: These methods combine information extracted from audio and video for deepfake detection. AVTS [39] concatenates modality-specific for Transformer-based classification, while MRDF [24] introduces crossand within-modality regularization. MAVPL [28] uses learnable prompt tokens to adapt frozen CLIP [40] and Whisper [41] encoders before aggregating their temporally aligned representations. KLASSify [42] calibrates modality-specific scores and combines them through max-out fusion. embeddings temporal b) Explicit cross-modal relation modeling: These methods examine audio-visual correspondence at different temporal and semantic levels. MDS [22] measures modality dissonance, AVAD [43] models synchronization anomalies, and LTI [27] examines attention-weighted local temporal distances. Other approaches focus on voice-face homogeneity [44], audiovisual speech agreement [26], and frame-level alignment [29]. c) Cross-modal representation fusion: Another direction uses information from one modality to update, predict, or reconstruct representations of the other. JAV-DFD [45] constructs synchronization stream through multi-level connections, while AVoiD-DF [46] and AVA-CL [47] employ bidirectional cross-attention. FGMDF [25] models neighboring audiovisual segments using heterogeneous graph. HOLA [48] and DigiShield [34] explore hierarchical contextual aggregation and spatiotemporal attention, respectively. FRADE [49] distills modality-agnostic audio information into the visual stream, while MCL [50] combines attention-based feature composition, contrastive learning, and frame-to-video distillation. In addition, AVFF [23], inspired by CAV-MAE [51], learns audio-visual representations through complementary masking and cross-modal reconstruction. PVASS-MDD [52] similarly uses cross-modal prediction and reconstruction, while AVAM [53] focuses on asynchrony-robust alignment and reconstruction. d) Explicit forensic-prior modeling: These methods incorporate semantic, behavioral, or generator-related evidence based on the properties of audio-visual synthesis. Specifically, CCFD [54] compares transcripts from audio and visual speech recognition to identify content inconsistencies. PIA [55] analyzes phoneme-conditioned articulation and temporal identity drift, while FauForensics [56] exploits facialaction-unit dynamics. To exploit generator-related evidence, X-AVDT [57] uses an inverted audio-conditioned diffusion model to extract reconstruction discrepancies and internal cross-attention patterns. In addition, EMO-Boost [58] models intraand inter-modal emotional dynamics and integrates them with an existing detector. Preprint

B. Deepfake Datasets Unimodal audio and visual datasets have supported deepfake detection research and the development of practical countermeasures for synthetic speech, voice conversion, and facial manipulations [59][61], [65][67], [72]. As generation technologies advance, audio-visual forgeries pose growing threat by manipulating both spoken content and visual appearance. FakeAVCeleb [30], an early dataset dedicated to multimodal deepfake detection, combines speech synthesis, face swapping, and lip synchronization to support research on manipulations affecting either or both modalities. Subsequent datasets have developed along two complementary directions: temporal forgery localization and broader coverage for deepfake classification. a) Temporal localization: LAV-DF [31] introduces localized, content-driven manipulations that change the meaning of spoken content. Following this line of research, AVDeepfake1M [35] substantially expands the dataset scale and uses large language model to generate diverse semantic modifications through word replacements, insertions, and deletions. AV-Deepfake1M++ [36] further broadens this coverage by expanding the manipulation strategies and introducing audiovisual perturbations. In addition, ArEnAV [77] applies similar operations to Arabic-English code-switching and dialectal variation. b) Deepfake classification: Datasets for deepfake classification cover an expanding range of languages and generation techniques. PolyGlotFake [32] and ILLUSION [78] broaden linguistic coverage through multilingual synthesis and multimodal manipulations. MAVOS-DD [79] evaluates generalization to unseen languages and generators, while ArEnAV [77] addresses Arabic-English code-switching and dialectal variation, supporting both classification and temporal localization. Alongside these linguistic extensions, DigiFakeAV [34] extends coverage beyond conventional face swapping to diffusion-based digital humans by combining synthesized speech with audio-driven video generation. Related resources also broaden the range of generated facial videos available for audio-visual detection: TalkingHeadBench [73] focuses on modern talking-head generators and changes in speaker identity and generation method, whereas MMDF [57] incorporates diverse facial generation methods based on adversarial learning, diffusion, and flow matching. Deepfake Detection Benchmarks Standardized benchmarks provide common basis for reproducible deepfake detection research. In the visual domain, DeepfakeBench [80] and ForensicHub [81] provide unified implementations and evaluation procedures for deepfake detection and broader image forensic tasks. MEGA-MMDF: DIVERSE MILLION-SCALE MULTIMODAL DEEPFAKE DATASET We introduce Mega-MMDF, million-scale audio-visual deepfake dataset with diverse forgery methods and pipelines. It contains 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips, constructed using 30 generation methods spanning eight forgery types and organized into 22 forgery pipelines. Real Data Collection We collect real audio-visual clips from VoxCeleb2 [85], MEAD [86], and CelebV-HQ [87], covering different recording environments, resolutions, and speaker demographics. To balance the representation of the selected demographic groups, we organize the clips into eight groups based on two gender categories and four skin-tone categories. These categories are used for dataset balancing and group-wise evaluation and do not exhaustively represent demographic diversity. The demographic labels were initially assigned using multimodal large language model (MLLM) and subsequently inspected and corrected manually for apparent labeling errors. Within each demographic group, we organize the selected real clips into disjoint pairs, with each clip belonging to exactly one pair. Each pair provides two directional sourcetarget assignments for constructing the forgery variants. We retain these pairs across pipelines and use them as the unit for dataset partitioning. B. Forgery Pipeline Construction Audio-visual deepfakes can be constructed by sequentially applying multiple generation or manipulation steps, resulting in stacked forgeries. For example, synthesized face can be animated using generated speech, while face-swapped video can undergo further reenactment to match new audio track. We define forgery method as specific generation algorithm that performs an operation on given inputs to produce an output. forgery pipeline specifies the selection and order of these operations, each implemented by corresponding method. We construct 22 forgery pipelines with the aim of producing audio-visual deepfakes without obvious mismatches between speech and lip movements. Depending on the pipeline, audio and visual content may be retained or manipulated, with audiodriven face reenactment applied when needed to establish the intended audiolip correspondence. We also include joint audio-video generation, which produces both modalities directly from text prompts. Table II summarizes the pipeline compositions. Specifically, these pipelines draw on the following four components. Audio forgery. We employ 10 methods covering Text-toSpeech synthesis (TTS), Voice Conversion (VC), and Partial Fake (PF). In particular, TTS generates speech from text using reference voice, whereas VC changes speaker characteristics while aiming to preserve the linguistic content. PF modifies selected portions of an utterance, such as individual words, while retaining the surrounding authentic speech. These methods comprise 5 TTS, 3 VC, and 2 PF methods. Visual forgery. We employ 12 methods covering Face Swapping (FS), Entire Face Synthesis (EFS), and Face Editing (FE). FS replaces facial identity while aiming to preserve the target videos expression, head pose, and surrounding content. EFS generates synthetic facial image, while FE modifies selected facial attributes, such as glasses or hair color. We use 4 FS, 5 EFS, and 3 FE methods. Audio-driven face reenactment. We incorporate 6 audiodriven face reenactment (FR) methods to animate facial images or adapt facial motion in videos to the accompanying audio. This stage enables image-based synthesis and editing methods to produce audio-visual clips. It also supports pipelines in which generated speech requires corresponding changes in visual content. Joint audio-video generation. To cover recent joint generation systems, we incorporate 2 Text-to-Audio-Video (T2AV) methods that generate audio and video together from text prompts. Together, these components support both individual forgery operations and stacked forgeries that combine multiple operations in sequence. For example, synthesized face can be animated through FR, or face swapping can be followed by reenactment driven by generated speech. The appendix provides complete list of generation methods (Table VIII), construction diagrams for each pipeline (Figs. 2833), and examples of generated clips (Figs. 3436). C. Annotations and Dataset Partitioning We assign each clip audio and visual authenticity labels, defining four combinations: real audio and real video (RARV), real audio and fake video (RAFV), fake audio and real video (FARV), and fake audio and fake video (FAFV). For clips generated using PF, the clip-level label indicates the presence of forgery in the corresponding modality, while temporal annotations specify the manipulated interval. The accompanying metadata records the generation methods used for forged clips and the source-file references for real clips. Clip identifiers and the dataset organization also identify the forgery pipeline and demographic group. In addition, generation prompts are retained for T2AV clips. We partition the dataset at the pair level. Within each demographic group, pairs are assigned to the training, validation, and test sets in 6:2:2 ratio. Each selected real clip is used without further subdivision and belongs to exactly one pair. Both real clips in pair and all generated clips associated with that pair are kept in the same split across pipelines, preventing cross-split reuse of the selected source clips and their forgery variants. The final dataset contains 1.3 million clips spanning 1,864 hours, with an average duration of 5.162 Preprint 6 Fig. 2. Modular Codebase of DeepfakeBench-MM seconds. Detailed statistics by pipeline, demographic group, and partition are provided in Section A.5. D. Ethics and Responsible Release To respect the access and distribution terms of the source datasets, Mega-MMDF will provide source-file indices for real clips rather than redistribute the corresponding media. Users must obtain these clips through the official access channels of the source datasets and comply with their applicable terms. To access the released media, users will need to register with valid email address and accept research-use agreement that prohibits malicious impersonation and deceptive dissemination. We will maintain dedicated channel for privacy and rightsrelated removal requests. Upon verification, we will remove affected clips and associated derivatives from distribution channels under our control. Registered users will also be notified and requested to delete the corresponding local copies. We will version dataset releases and document changes to support the traceability of experimental results. Source-specific licensing information and further details of the release policy are provided in Sections A.1 and A.2. IV. DEEPFAKEBENCH-MM: UNIFIED AND INTEGRATED BENCHMARK FOR MM-DFD To assess the training value of Mega-MMDF and compare detector behavior under common experimental setup, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, unified benchmark supporting 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Its modular codebase provides common experimental infrastructure while accommodating detector-specific requirements and configurations. A. Modular Codebase As illustrated in Fig. 2, the codebase comprises six modules connected through shared interfaces. The preprocessing module standardizes data preprocessing and dataset organization, while the data-loading module constructs inputs according to detector-specific configurations. The detector module encapsulates model architectures and training objectives, and the training module manages optimization, validation, and checkpoint selection. The evaluation module implements common evaluation protocols, while the analysis module provides tools for inspecting predictions and learned representations. This organization supports extension through dataset-specific preprocessing adapters and loading configurations, detector implementations following the shared interface, and additional metrics and analysis tools within their respective modules. Implementation details and configuration options are provided in Appendix B. B. Supported Datasets and Detectors a) Datasets: DeepfakeBench-MM supports 8 multimodal deepfake datasets: FakeAVCeleb [30], LAV-DF [31], PolyGlotFake [32], IDForge [33], TalkingHeadBench [73], DigiFakeAV [34], MMDF [57], and our Mega-MMDF. These datasets differ in storage formats, directory structures, media characteristics, and forgery annotations. To support consistent access across datasets, the preprocessing module standardizes their organization and annotations. We also exclude the initial interval corresponding to two video frames from both modalities to reduce potential reliance on the leading-silence artifacts identified in [29]. For training and inference, the data-loading module samples fixed-length temporal windows from variable-length audio-visual clips. Each window forms an input instance, with its duration, video sampling rate, audio representation, and other settings determined by the requirements of each detector. Preprocessing and data-loading details are provided in Sections B.1 and B.2. b) Detectors: The detector module integrates 10 multimodal detectors, divided into two categories. (1) Trainingbased detectors: We implement baseline comprising an audio backbone, visual backbone, and an MLP classifier, together with 6 existing models: AVFF [23], AVH [29], FRADE [49], FGMDF [25], FauForensics [56], and MCL [50]. For methods without complete public implementations, we request code or implementation guidance from the authors, or reproduce the models based on their published descriptions. (2) Trainingfree detectors: We include SpeechForensics [26], Qwen2.5Omni [88], and VideoLLaMA2.1 [89] to examine the applicability of pretrained audio-visual representations and multimodal large language models to deepfake detection without additional training on the benchmark datasets. The detector module connects these methods to the shared evaluation and analysis modules through standardized outputs. The details of the implementation are provided in Section B.3. A. Training Value of Mega-MMDF We first evaluate the overall training benefits of MegaMMDF compared with existing datasets. We then investigate the factors underlying these benefits by examining the effects of training data scale and the importance of forgery-pipeline coverage. Q1: Does training on Mega-MMDF improve detection performance? To compare the effectiveness of different training datasets, we train each detector separately on FakeAVCeleb, LAV-DF, PolyGlotFake, IDForge, and Mega-MMDF. For each detector, we keep its training configuration consistent across training datasets, following the benchmark protocol described in Section IV. We evaluate each resulting model on the same eight test datasets and report their mean clip-level AUCs. As shown in Table IV, training on Mega-MMDF achieves the highest mean AUC for all seven detectors. Compared with the strongest alternative training dataset for each detector, the improvements range from 0.0085 to 0.0784. These consistent improvements across different architectures demonstrate the overall effectiveness of Mega-MMDF as training resource. We first examine how detectors trained on existing datasets perform across the pipelines in Mega-MMDF. We then conduct complementary experiment within Mega-MMDF, using common source of real data to test whether training on single pipeline provides broad cross-pipeline coverage. In the first experiment, we evaluate the previously trained detectors separately on each Mega-MMDF pipeline. Each evaluation pairs the fake test clips from one pipeline with the same real test clips and reports clip-level AUC. Fig. 4 presents AVH as an example; results for the other detectors are provided in Figs. 22 and 23 in the appendix. Training on existing datasets produces uneven performance across pipelines, with clear weaknesses that are not apparent from the aggregate scores alone. For example, AVH trained on LAV-DF obtains AUCs of 0.510 and 0.456 on P7 and P8, and 0.446 and 0.411 on P19 and P20. Although IDForge includes additional faceswapping and voice-conversion pipelines, training on it only partially addresses these gaps, with weaknesses remaining on P1, P3, and P4. Performance on the emerging T2AV pipeline also varies considerably across training datasets. These results indicate that existing training resources provide incomplete coverage of the diverse forgery conditions represented in Mega-MMDF. For each single-pipeline training run, we select one checkpoint with the highest clip-level AUC on an in-domain validation set comprising fake clips from the same pipeline and real clips from P0. We evaluate six transformations: H.264 and AAC compression simulate lossy video and audio encoding, respectively; video downsampling reduces spatial resolution; frame loss and audio dropout simulate missing video frames and audio segments; and audio-visual offsets introduce temporal misalignment. Detailed settings are provided in Section B.5 and Table XI. Fig. 11 reports changes in clip-level AUC relative to the clean condition. The top row shows results for the seven Mega-MMDF-trained detectors evaluated on Mega-MMDF. The bottom row reports average AUC changes across the other seven datasets for these detectors and across all eight datasets for the three training-free methods. Sensitivity varies across transformations and detectors. For the trained detectors, video compression and audio dropout cause noticeable degradation on Mega-MMDF, while audio compression and dropout produce larger average losses across the other seven datasets. Downsampling, frame loss, and temporal offsets generally have smaller effects within the tested ranges. Among the training-free methods, SpeechForensics shows pronounced decline under video compression. In contrast, Qwen2.5-Omni and VideoLLaMA2.1 exhibit smaller changes in average AUC, with absolute changes below 0.013 across all tested transformations and severity levels. These results show that robustness depends on the transformation and that robustness observed on Mega-MMDF does not necessarily extend to other datasets, highlighting the importance of evaluating cross-dataset robustness under different post-processing conditions. Q9: How does detection performance vary across demographic groups? We evaluate the seven Mega-MMDF-trained detectors and three training-free methods on the Mega-MMDF test split. Following [90], we report four fairness metrics: demographic parity (DP), equal odds (EO), overall accuracy equality (OAE), and maximum equalized odds (MEO), all evaluated at fixed decision threshold of 0.5. We also report SDAUC [91], defined as the standard deviation of clip-level AUC across the eight demographic groups. The thresholdbased metrics assess disparities in prediction rates or classification performance across groups, while SDAUC measures variation in ranking performance. Detailed definitions are provided in Section B.5. Table VII reports demographic disparities under these five metrics. Among the training-based detectors, FRADE achieves the lowest DP, OAE, and SDAUC, while FauForensics achieves the lowest EO and MEO. SpeechForensics obtains zero DP, EO, and MEO because it classifies all clips as real at the threshold of 0.5. Its AUC nevertheless varies across demographic groups, yielding an SDAUC of 0.0199. This example shows that low threshold-based disparities can coexist with failure to detect forgeries at the chosen threshold. VI. CONCLUSION In this work, we introduce Mega-MMDF, million-scale multimodal deepfake dataset covering 30 forgery methods and 22 forgery pipelines, and develop DeepfakeBench-MM to evaluate its training value and systematically investigate detector behavior under unified experimental settings. Future work will expand Mega-MMDFs forgery coverage and extend DeepfakeBench-MM with additional detectors and evaluation protocols. Our experiments demonstrate the advantages of MegaMMDF as training source under the benchmark protocol and support the value of data scale and pipeline diversity. Using Mega-MMDF as common experimental foundation, we compare detectors and reveal bidirectional and asymmetric cross-pipeline generalization, showing that training on composite pipelines does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. False alarms and missed forgeries under the evaluated missing-modality conditions motivate modality-flexible detection, while responses to temporal misalignment motivate further study of how audio-visual correspondence is defined, learned, and used for detection. Post-processing robustness and demographic disparity evaluations provide protocols and reference results for subsequent research.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: This appendix provides additional details on Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM. Appendix details the datasets ethics and release policy, licenses and usage terms of the source and benchmark datasets, forgery methods and pipelines, and dataset statistics. Appendix documents the benchmarks modular implementation, experimental configurations, and additional evaluation and analysis results. A. ADDITIONAL DETAILS ON MEGA-MMDF This section documents the construction, release, and assessment of Mega-MMDF. We first discuss ethical considerations and responsible release policies, followed by the licenses and usage terms of the datasets used for construction and benchmark evaluation. We then summarize the generation methods within each forgery category and illustrate how they are combined into individual pipelines, including the provenance of their inputs. Finally, we present dataset statistics covering its composition and training, validation, and test partitions. A.1 Mega-MMDF Ethics and Responsible Release Mega-MMDF is intended for research on multimodal deepfake detection. To support responsible use and mitigate potential misuse, we adopt the access and dataset maintenance policies described below. a) Data provenance and access policy: We will provide source indices and reconstruction scripts instead of redistributing real clips. Users must obtain the corresponding real source clips from the respective providers, and reconstruct the complete dataset locally. The applicable source-dataset licenses and usage agreements are summarized in Section A.2. Access to the media distributed through Mega-MMDF will require email verification and data-use agreement signed by all researchers requesting access. Applications will record their names, institutional affiliations, and contact information to support access management, documentation of agreement acceptance, and subsequent update notifications. b) Privacy requests and dataset maintenance: We will maintain dedicated contact channel for privacy and rightsrelated removal requests from individuals depicted in the dataset, their authorized representatives, and relevant rights holders. Upon verification, we will remove the affected clips and associated derivatives identified through our provenance records from the distribution channels under our control. Each removal update will be assigned new release version, accompanied by record of affected clip identifiers and cleanup utility for users to update local copies. When the update is issued, all registered users who have signed the Mega-MMDF data-use agreement will be notified by email and required to remove the affected clips. Users will be required to report the release version of our Mega-MMDF used in their experiments, together with any subsequent removal updates applied, so that the documented dataset composition can be checked for inclusion of affected clips. Once removed, affected clips will no longer be accessible through our MegaMMDF data release platform. A.2 Licenses of Utilized Datasets The datasets used in this work fall into two categories: realdata sources for constructing Mega-MMDF and existing deepfake datasets incorporated into DeepfakeBench-MM. For each category, we first summarize the licenses, usage agreements, and access conditions published by the dataset providers, and then describe the corresponding usage and distribution practices adopted in this work. Official license and policy documents are referenced in the footnotes. A.2.1 Real-Data

This section describes its six modules: data preprocessing, data loading, detector, training, evaluation, and analysis. B.1 Preprocessing Module Audiovisual datasets differ in media formats, frame rates, audio sampling rates, directory structures, and annotation formats. The preprocessing module converts source audiovisual clips and their annotations into aligned face videos, resampled audio, facial landmarks, and metadata in common format. a) Framework and Extensibility: The module combines shared clip-processing procedure with dataset-specific adapters. The shared procedure performs face detection, continuous-sequence selection, and face alignment. Each adapter reads the datasets files and annotations, prepares the required inputs, and organizes the outputs. For each dataset, dataset-specific code reads its directory structure and annotations to construct list of clips. Each entry specifies the source file path, the output location, the split assignment, and the available labels and manipulation intervals. The shared clip-level procedure processes these entries, and successfully processed recordings are collected into split-specific metadata files. Support for new dataset requires extracting these inputs from its original files and annotations. The shared faceprocessing procedure and output format remain the same. This organization allows additional datasets with different file layouts or annotation formats to use the existing preprocessing and data-loading code. In addition, different trainvalidationtest partitions can change the difficulty of an evaluation and make results from separate studies difficult to compare. To reduce this source of variation, DeepfakeBench-MM uses fixed partitions across detectors for datasets such as FakeAVCeleb [30], PolyGlotFake [32], and DigiFakeAV [34], where official dataset splits are unavailable. The corresponding split information will accompany the benchmark release to support reproducible comparisons. e) Dataset Availability and Future Extensions: To the best of our knowledge, test-set annotations specifying manipulation intervals for AVDeepfake1M [35] and AVDeepfake1M++ [36] have not been publicly released at the time of writing. Without temporal annotations, we cannot reliably assign authenticity labels to the windows selected after preprocessing and during data loading. Therefore, these datasets are not included in our DeepfakeBench-MM. At the time of writing, access requests, downloading, and preprocessing for DeepSpeak [76], KoDF [69], and ArEnAV [77] are still in progress. We plan to extend the benchmark to these datasets as the necessary access, annotations, and processing become available, and to additional audio visual face deepfake datasets in the future. If the source datasets license and any required permissions explicitly allow redistribution of processed data, we also plan to provide preprocessed versions to users whose authorization to access the source dataset has been verified. Otherwise, users can run the scripts on their own authorized copies. This release strategy aims to reduce repeated preprocessing effort and facilitate subsequent research. B.2 Data Loading Module The data-loading module reads the standardized outputs of the preprocessing module and constructs detector-specific input instances from preprocessed audiovisual clips. Each instance consists of video frames and the corresponding audio segment sampled from temporal window, together with its labels and metadata. shared loading interface supports detector-specific input formats through configuration files. a) Framework and Extensibility: Temporal sampling is defined separately for training, validation, and testing. Let denote the number of frames in preprocessed clip, the number of frames loaded per input instance, and the frame stride. Each instance occupies window of frames, corresponding to s/25 seconds at the preprocessing frame rate of 25 frames per second. For training and validation, the preprocessed audiovisual clip is divided into = min(M, N/(T s)) approximately equal temporal partitions, where is configurable maximum number of instances per clip for training and validation, and is set to two in our detector configurations. Training randomly selects complete window within each partition. This allows the detector to receive different temporal windows of the same clip across epochs. Validation instead selects fixed window starting at each partition boundary. Using small number of fixed windows reduces validation time and resource consumption while keeping temporal sampling deterministic. Testing places complete windows consecutively along the preprocessed clips without overlap. It produces N/(T s) input instances and discards remaining frames that cannot form complete instance window. This strategy covers as much of the clip as possible using complete, non-overlapping windows, without padding the final video window with zeros or repeating inference over overlapping windows. clip 27https://deepfakes1m.github.io/2024/details; https://deepfakes1m.github.io/ 2025/details shorter than one window contributes no input instances in any split. The reading configuration specifies the visual resolution, RGB or grayscale format, frame stride, and pixel normalization mean and standard deviation. For audio, it specifies the target sampling rate and whether to return waveform or extracted features. Supported feature types include STFT, Mel, Log-Mel, and MFCC. Feature extraction settings and optional spectral normalization depend on the selected backend, e.g., torchaudio, librosa, python_speech_features. The audio segment is read from the same temporal window as the video window. Dataset manifests provide paths, split membership, and authenticity labels, together with manipulation intervals and demographic annotations when available. Datasets following this format can use the same loading procedure. Additional input representations or sampling policies can be implemented in the corresponding loading utilities without changing the detectors forward computation. The module also provides processing hooks for training augmentation, robustness evaluation, and modality masking. Their settings are described in Sections B.4 and B.5. b) Input Configurations: Table IX lists the input configurations used by the evaluated detectors. Spatial sizes and frame counts refer to the loader outputs. Additional frame selection, cropping, and other model-specific input operations are described below the table. c) Labels and Metadata: Each instance retains its source path and temporal coordinates, joint and modality-specific authenticity labels, and available demographic annotations. Optional landmarks are loaded using the same indices as the video frames. For partially manipulated sequences, the manifest preserves manipulation intervals so that labels can account for the selected window. Frame-level visual labels indicate whether each sampled frame lies within manipulated interval. The binary instance label is positive when either modality is labeled as manipulated. B.3 Detector Module Audiovisual deepfake detectors use different feature extractors, fusion methods, and training objectives. The detector module provides common interface for running these detectors within the benchmark. It receives the inputs prepared by the data-loading module, computes features and authenticity predictions, and provides the losses required for training. a) Framework and Extensibility: Each detector implements feature extraction, classification, and loss computation through the same interface. During forward pass, it reads the audio and video inputs and returns prediction scores together with any features needed for its losses or subsequent analysis. During training, its loss function uses these outputs and the corresponding labels to compute an overall loss and individual loss terms. The training and evaluation modules can therefore call different detectors through the same interface while each detector retains its own architecture and objective. This structure supports different audio and visual encoders, fusion operations, and combinations of joint and modality-specific supervision. Separate detector configurations can also support different stages of training procedure, such as pretraining and subsequent classification. b) Detectors Included in This Study: We include vanilla Baseline and six existing detectors: AVFF [23], AVH [29], FGMDF [25], FRADE [49], FauForensics [56], and MCL [50]. In the following, we summarize their backbones, key modules, and training objectives. The input configurations and training settings are provided in Table IX and Section B.4, respectively. We denote commonly used cross-entropy losses for joint, audio, and video authenticity classification by Lav CE, and Lv CE, La CE. c) Baseline: Our baseline uses 3D ResNet-18 video encoder and an SE-ResNet audio encoder. Temporal averaging on features produces one 512-dimensional vector in either modality. Their concatenation is passed to an MLP consisting of 512-dimensional hidden layer, batch normalization, ReLU activation, dropout with probability 0.5, and two-class output layer. The model is trained with joint cross-entropy, Lav CE. d) AVFF: AVFF [23] follows two-stage learning procedure with MARLIN [114] and AudioMAE [115] as the video and audio backbones. The first stage learns audiovisual correspondence from real data. Complementary Masking hides different temporal portions of the two modalities, so that masked portion in one modality remains visible in the other. Audio-to-video and video-to-audio mappings provide crossmodal features to reconstruct the masked content. The pretraining objective combines an audiovisual contrastive loss, Lc, with reconstruction and adversarial losses, Lrec and Ladv. The contrastive loss brings paired audio and video representations closer, while reconstruction and adversarial training encourage the features to preserve the information needed to recover the missing content. Generator and discriminator updates alternate during adversarial pretraining. The second stage uses the pretrained encoders and crossmodal mappings without complementary masking. Original and cross-modal features are combined and passed to an MLP classification head. Training with Lav CE adapts the learned representations to final decisions. e) AVH: We adopt the supervised variant of AVH, termed AVH-sup in the original paper [29], and refer to it as AVH in this benchmark. frozen AVHuBERT [113] backbone extracts audio and visual features separately. An MLP scores the paired features at each time step, and log-sum-exp pooling aggregates the temporal scores into prediction for the input window. Our implementation uses two-class output trained with Lav CE. f) FGMDF: FGMDF [25] represents audio and video features as heterogeneous graph. convolutional visual encoder and waveform encoder based on sinc filtering and residual blocks extract modality-specific features. Cross-modal graph interaction exchanges information between audio and Preprint 25 visual nodes to capture their temporal relationships. Graph attention aggregates the node features, while De-homogenization Graph Pooling removes redundant nodes to preserve diverse graph-level information. We retain the audio and video classification heads and use binary joint head for this benchmark. The training objective is LFGMDF = Lv CE + La CE + Lav CE, (3) which encourages the model to identify both modality-specific forgeries and the overall authenticity of an audiovideo pair. g) FRADE: FRADE [49] uses shared ViT-B/16 backbone to process visual frames and audio spectrograms. Its Adaptive Forgery-aware Injection (AFI) module extracts highfrequency cues and injects them into attention computations, allowing modality-specific forgery information to influence the pretrained features. Its Audio-distilled Cross-modal Interaction (ACI) module uses learnable latent tokens to extract information from audio before interacting with visual features. This intermediate representation is intended to reduce interference from modality-specific information when learning audio visual inconsistencies. The resulting audio and visual features are fused for classification. The original method freezes the pretrained ViT and learns the added modules. The training objective combines three terms: LFRADE = Lav CE + 0.3LCMC + 0.4LCC. (4) The Cross-modal Contrastive Loss, LCMC, brings audio and visual features closer for authentic pairs and penalizes their similarity above margin for manipulated pairs. The AudioVisual Center Cluster Loss, LCC, brings authentic fused features toward common center and encourages manipulated features to lie farther away. Together with authenticity classification, these objectives encourage compact authentic representations and separation from manipulated content. h) FauForensics: FauForensics [56] augments audio visual detection with Facial Action Unit (FAU) features. Our implementation uses CSN-101 video encoder, Whisper [41] audio encoder, and frozen MEFARG [116] FAU extractor with ResNet-50 backbone. FAU-enhanced Feature Learning combines facial-action features with visual features to capture subtle facial dynamics. Implicit Feature Alignment uses shared learnable queries to align the audio and visual representations. Temporal Attentional Pooler then captures relationships within and between the two modalities, and separate classifiers predict joint and modality-specific authenticity. The objective is LFauForensics = 0.8Lav CE + 0.1La CE + 0.1Lv CE. (5) The auxiliary audio and video losses provide direct supervision for each modality along with the joint detection objective. i) MCL: MCL [50] combines frame, video, and audio information through two training stages. The first stage trains an EfficientNet-B7 frame teacher with frame authenticity labels. The second freezes this teacher and learns the video and audio branches. Following the implementation provided by the authors, we use ViViT and Cnn14, respectively. Frame and video features are combined into framevideo representation, while an attention-based fusion module forms an audiovideo representation. These compositional features allow the model to use spatial forgery cues from the teacher together with temporal and cross-modal information. Multimodal contrastive learning uses authenticity labels to bring compatible representations closer and separate incompatible ones. The audio-related contrastive loss, LA, relates video features to audio and audiovideo features; the framerelated contrastive loss, LI , relates video features to frame and framevideo features. prediction-consistency term, Lcons, transfers information from the framevideo prediction to the video branch. The original paper defines this term as JensenShannon divergence loss, Ljsd. Noise-based Feature Augmentation (NFA) additionally perturbs fused features with learned multiplicative and additive noise during training to improve robustness to feature variation. Using the weights in our training configurations, the secondstage objective is LMCL = 2Lv CE + La CE + LA + LI + Lcons + Ldis + LNFA. (6) Here, Ldis classifies the audiovideo compositional features, and LNFA classifies the features after noise augmentation. The modality-specific classification losses retain supervision for audio and video, while the contrastive and consistency terms encourage information transfer across representations. Noise augmentation is disabled during inference. j) SpeechForensics: SpeechForensics [26] detects inconsistencies between the speech content conveyed by lip movements and the corresponding audio. We use the pretrained AVHuBERT-Large [113] checkpoint used by the official implementation. Its visual frontend is ResNet-18 with an initial 3D convolution, while linear projection processes stacked Log-Mel audio features. shared encoder with 24 Transformer blocks produces contextual speech representations. The original representation learning procedure uses authentic speech videos, with iteratively refined cluster assignments providing frame-level targets and masked prediction encouraging temporal context modeling. Modality dropout enables the encoder to process either modality independently. In our benchmark, the backbone remains frozen, with no benchmark-specific training or additional classification head. At inference, four consecutive Log-Mel feature frames are concatenated and layer-normalized before audio encoding. The model processes the mouth sequence and audio separately to obtain final-layer visual and audio embeddings. Following the official fixed time-offset alignment, we compute framewise cosine similarities for each integer offset from 15 to 15, with out-of-range audio embeddings set to zero. The matching score is the maximum of the temporally averaged similarities across these offsets, selecting one constant offset for the entire input window. Lower matching scores indicate greater audiovisual inconsistency. We convert this score to pfake = (1 S)/2 on the benchmarks [0, 1] scale without learning probability calibration. This procedure is applied to the non-overlapping 25-frame (1-second) windows specified in Table IX; the original evaluation instead uses whole-video inputs. k) Qwen2.5-Omni: Qwen2.5-Omni [88] is pretrained multimodal model with ThinkerTalker architecture. The Preprint 26 Thinker integrates visual and audio representations with text in an autoregressive language model, while the Talker supports speech generation. Time-aligned Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (TMRoPE) aligns the temporal positions of video and audio inputs. We use the Qwen2.5-Omni-7B checkpoint and only its Thinker for authenticity scoring; the speechgeneration branch is not used. All parameters remain frozen, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning or additional classification head. Each input consists of eight uniformly sampled RGB frames and the synchronized 16 kHz mono audio from non-overlapping 4-second window, as specified in Table IX. The checkpoint processor prepares the multimodal inputs and applies the models chat template. We use the prompt: Carefully analyze the video and audio to determine whether this audiovisual content is real or fake. Provide only single-word response: Real or Fake. Instead of sampling textual answer, we obtain the next-token logits for the single-token labels Real and Fake at the final attended prompt position. Denoting these logits by zReal and zFake, respectively, we compute the detection score as pfake = exp(zFake) exp(zReal) + exp(zFake) . (7) This two-label normalization produces continuous score for benchmark evaluation without fitting probability calibration to the test data. l) VideoLLaMA2.1: VideoLLaMA2.1 [89] combines modality-specific encoders with language model for audio visual understanding. We use the VideoLLaMA2.1-7B-AV checkpoint, which comprises SigLIP visual encoder, BEATs audio encoder, and Qwen2 language backbone. spatialtemporal convolutional connector aggregates visual features across frames and maps them into the language models embedding space. two-layer MLP with GELU activation projects the audio features into the same space, allowing the language backbone to jointly process the audio visual representations and the textual instruction. The audio branch uses 128-bin log-Mel filterbank features. As with Qwen2.5-Omni, we keep the pretrained model frozen and evaluate it in zero-shot setting without learned deepfake classification head. We use the same synchronized 4-second windows, eight uniformly sampled frames, 16 kHz mono audio, and detection prompt, with the checkpoints own visual preprocessing and chat template. The model processes both modalities in single forward pass, and we compute pfake from the next-token logits using Eq. 7. Our implementation applies the vocabulary projection only to the final attended hidden state, yielding the same next-token scores as projecting every sequence position while reducing intermediate memory usage. Neither model is optimized on the benchmark training split. B.5 Evaluation Module The evaluation module measures detection performance, demographic fairness, and robustness to post-processing through three evaluation protocols. It receives detector predictions together with their labels and metadata, and computes metrics for comparison across models and datasets. a) Framework and Extensibility: Detector inference and metric computation are handled separately. Prediction records contain source paths, sampled temporal intervals, authenticity scores, labels, and demographic annotations when available. These records can be reused to compute different metrics without repeating inference. common metric interface supports instance-level and clip-level evaluation. Additional metrics can be implemented through this interface, while additional testtime perturbations can be incorporated into the data-loading module. b) Detection Performance Evaluation: The benchmark currently implements four performance metrics: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), average precision (AP), accuracy (ACC), and equal error rate (EER). AUC is the primary metric in this study, while the other three provide complementary measurements. The metric interface can be extended to include balanced accuracy, precision, recall, and other evaluation criteria. ACC uses decision threshold of 0.5 by default, with scores greater than 0.5 classified as manipulated. EER is estimated at the empirical ROC operating point with the smallest absolute difference between the falsepositive and false-negative rates. Within-dataset evaluation measures performance on the held-out test split of the training dataset, whereas cross-dataset evaluation measures generalization to different dataset.
